title: Infrastructure Financing and Deal Structuring
notes: The heaviest week in the module and the one where the set texts are strongest. Gatti is the primary source throughout. Students should have read Gatti chapters 1 and 3 and Delmon chapters 1 and 2 before the session.
text: RE07 Global Infrastructure Investment and Management Week 4 Infrastructure Financing and Deal Structuring Professor Helen X. H. Bao Department of Land Economy, University of Cambridge Guest session: International Finance Corporation

title: What this week does
notes: If you have only fifty minutes, run A, the risk matrix in C, and one case from G. Everything else can be picked up in supervision.
text: What this week does Weeks 2 and 3 established who decides and who pays. This week is about the instrument that connects them: a contract, or rather a network of contracts, that converts a physical asset into a stream of payments reliable enough to borrow against. The syllabus asks specifically for a comparison of project finance with corporate finance and for cases from both advanced and developing economies, and the week is built around that structure. 2 A Project finance against corporate finance 35 min B The special purpose vehicle and its contracts 35 min C Risk identification and allocation 40 min D Sources of funds and the capital stack 40 min E Procurement routes and how the deal is won 30 min F Public support, guarantees and credit enhancement 30 min G Two cases: Murcia and Odebrecht 35 min

title: What you already have
notes: The environmental policy row is the strongest isomorphism in the module and worth ten minutes rather than a mention. Ask an EP student to state the instrument choice problem, then map it onto the delivery models.
text: What you already have Where this week draws on modules you have taken, or are taking now. Nothing below is assumed: each idea is stated in full before the module is named. 3 Your programme Where it was taught What it gives this week Real Estate Finance RE01 sessions 2 to 4, corporate finance, capital structure and the weighted average cost of capital; sessions 6 and 7, financial and real options. RE03 weeks 2, 6 and 7, risk, feasibility and funding the project. Project finance is capital structure theory at its limit: a single-asset firm with very high leverage and a contractual network standing in for covenants. RE03 follows the same sequence for a building. Planning, Growth and Regeneration PGR01 Lent lecture 9, planning for growth and land value capture. PGR02 Michaelmas week 8, land value capture. PGR07 lecture 3, financing mechanisms behind regeneration. PGR04 lecture 4, rent-seeking. Where the money comes from when there is no user charge, and why a contract signed after competition is renegotiated afterwards. Environmental Policy EP02, elements of the theory of environmental policy I to III; environmental policy under asymmetric information; policy under risk and the use of liability rules. EP06 lectures 7 and 8, push and pull instruments. Choosing between procurement, concession and availability payment is the same problem as choosing between a tax, a quantity instrument and a property right: which instrument delivers the outcome at least cost given what the principal cannot observe. Everyone RM01 lectures 1 to 4, regression and model specification. A financial mode

title: Project finance against corporate finance
blockname: Project finance against corporate finance
notes: Start from the comparison the syllabus asks for. Everything in the week follows from the two or three features that make project finance distinct.
text: Block A Project finance against corporate finance What is actually different, and why the difference is worth its cost. Indicative length 35 minutes 4

title: A definition worth being precise about
blockname: Project finance against corporate finance
notes: Make students state the definition back. The three components map onto the three blocks that follow.
text: A definition worth being precise about Project finance is the financing of a single-purpose entity on the strength of the cash flow that entity is expected to generate, with limited or no recourse to the sponsors who created it. The lenders look to the project rather than to a balance sheet, and their security is the project itself together with the contracts that produce its revenue. That definition contains the whole subject. Single purpose means no other business to contaminate or to support. Cash flow means the asset must be contracted or regulated well enough to be forecast. Limited recourse means the sponsor’s loss is capped at its equity, which is why the structure exists at all. A Gatti, ch. 1.1; Esty, B. C. (2004), European Financial Management 10(2), 213–224. 5

title: The comparison the syllabus asks for
blockname: Project finance against corporate finance
notes: This is the table Abor chapter 13 provides and it is the spine of the block. The last row is the one to dwell on: project finance does not reduce risk, it relocates it and makes the relocation explicit.
text: The comparison the syllabus asks for A Abor and others (2025), ch. 13, table 13.1; Gatti, ch. 1.2. 6 Corporate finance Project finance Borrower An operating company with many assets A special purpose vehicle with one Basis of credit The balance sheet and historic earnings Forecast cash flow from a single asset Leverage Moderate, constrained by the business risk High, often seventy per cent or more Security General claims, sometimes secured Project assets, contracts, accounts and shares Control of cash Management discretion A payment waterfall with lock-up tests Recourse to owners Full, within the company Limited, and defined by contract Cost of arranging Low Very high, in both fees and time Where risk sits Diversified across the firm Allocated by contract to named parties

title: Why a sponsor would accept the cost
blockname: Project finance against corporate finance
notes: The final bullet is the answer to the obvious student question, which is why anybody would do this. Below a certain size it is not rational and the sponsor should use its balance sheet.
text: Why a sponsor would accept the cost Risk containment. A failure is confined to the vehicle and does not reach the sponsor’s other businesses, which matters most where a single project is large relative to the sponsor. Higher leverage. Contracted cash flow supports debt that a corporate balance sheet could not, which raises the return on the equity committed. Off balance sheet treatment, where the accounting permits it, though this is far more constrained than it once was and is a weak reason on its own. Risk sharing with partners. A consortium can undertake a project none of its members would attempt alone. Discipline. High leverage and a tight covenant package constrain management discretion, which is the agency argument Jensen made about debt generally. Against all of this sits the cost: arranging a project financing takes eighteen months and a great deal of money, and it is worth it only for large, long-lived, contractually stable assets. A Gatti, ch. 1.2 and 1.5. 7

title: The theory: separation, and the conflicts it creates
blockname: Project finance against corporate finance
notes: This is the analytical frame for blocks B and D. Wealth expropriation between claimants is the problem the entire structure is designed against.
text: The theory: separation, and the conflicts it creates Gatti sets out the academic account. Separate incorporation avoids contamination risk in both directions: the project cannot drag down the sponsor and the sponsor’s difficulties cannot reach the project. High leverage and a single asset then create a sharp conflict between sponsors and lenders, because equity holders in a highly geared vehicle have an incentive to take risk whose upside they capture and whose downside falls on lenders. Every structural feature students meet this week is a response to that conflict: the covenant package, the reserve accounts, the lock-up tests, the restrictions on distributions, and the security over shares that lets lenders take the project away. A Gatti, ch. 1.5; Esty (2004). 8

title: The empirical validation, by the author of the set text
blockname: Project finance against corporate finance
notes: The single best justification for spending block B on contracts. Structure is not documentation, it is basis points.
text: The empirical validation, by the author of the set text 2,000+ Project finance loans used to test whether the network of non-financial contracts around a vehicle measurably affects its financing. Corielli, Gatti and Steffanoni ask whether the contractual architecture is doing real work or is merely legal ritual. They find it is doing real work. A well-designed set of contracts that pre-commits the actions of construction contractors, operators, suppliers and offtakers reduces loan spreads and supports higher debt-to-equity ratios. In other words, lenders read the contracts, price them, and lend more against a project whose counterparties are properly bound. For students this converts an apparently descriptive topic into a quantitative one. Contract design has a price, and the price is observable. A Corielli, F., Gatti, S. and Steffanoni, A. (2010), Journal of Money, Credit and Banking 42(7), 1295–1320. 9

title: Where the technique came from
blockname: Project finance against corporate finance
notes: The last sentence is the analytical payload. An availability payment exists to give a hospital the contractual shape of a power station.
text: Where the technique came from Project finance is old. Lending against the output of a specific venture, with recourse limited to that venture, was used for maritime trade and for mining long before it acquired the name. Its modern form developed in North Sea oil and in independent power generation, where the assets were large, the output was contracted to a creditworthy buyer, and the sponsors were unwilling to place the whole exposure on their balance sheets. That history explains the shape of the technique. It was built for assets with a single identifiable output sold under a long contract, which is why it fits power and process plant naturally, transport with more difficulty, and social infrastructure only once availability payments were invented to manufacture the missing contract. A Gatti, ch. 2.1. 10

title: Where it is used, and why the pattern looks as it does
blockname: Project finance against corporate finance
notes: The bottom row is the current frontier and the least settled. Lenders are being asked to price a twenty-year exposure to an industry whose technology turns over in five.
text: Where it is used, and why the pattern looks as it does A Gatti, ch. 2.1 and 2.2; Abor and others (2025), ch. 13. 11 Sector Fit with the technique Why Power generation Very strong A single measurable output sold to one buyer under a long contract Renewables Very strong As above, with a subsidy or contract for difference supplying the offtake Oil, gas and process Strong Large, contracted, and sponsored by counterparties with the capacity to support Transport with availability payments Strong The state manufactures the contracted revenue that demand risk would deny Toll roads and airports Moderate Demand risk sits with the project, so leverage is lower and pricing wider Water and social infrastructure Moderate Contracted, but with a public counterparty and heavy political exposure Digital and data centres Growing Contracted to strong tenants, but with a technology cycle far shorter than the debt

title: When not to use project finance
blockname: Project finance against corporate finance
notes: Students often leave a course like this believing project finance is always the sophisticated answer. It usually is not.
text: When not to use project finance Where the project is small relative to the sponsor, because the arranging cost cannot be recovered. Where revenue cannot be contracted or regulated, because there is nothing to size debt against. Where the technology is unproven, since lenders will not take technology risk at any price and the sponsor ends up guaranteeing it anyway. Where speed matters, because eighteen months to financial close is normal and cannot easily be compressed. Where the sponsor has cheap balance sheet capacity and no reason to ring-fence, in which case corporate debt is simply cheaper. The honest summary is that project finance is expensive machinery justified only by scale, contractual stability and a genuine need to contain risk. A 12

title: Block A discussion
blockname: Project finance against corporate finance
text: Block A discussion Seminar questions A utility with a strong balance sheet is building a plant that is small relative to its assets. Should it use project finance? What changes your answer? Project finance carries high arranging costs and takes far longer. Under what conditions does the leverage benefit outweigh that, and how would you test it? Corielli and colleagues find that contract quality moves loan spreads. What does that imply about who should be in the room when the project agreements are drafted? A 13

title: The special purpose vehicle and its contracts
blockname: The special purpose vehicle and its contracts
notes: Draw the structure diagram on the board and build it up contract by contract. It is the most useful single hour in the module for students going into practice.
text: Block B The special purpose vehicle and its contracts One company, no employees, and a web of agreements that produce a bankable cash flow. Indicative length 35 minutes 14

title: A company built to be predictable
blockname: The special purpose vehicle and its contracts
notes: The framing sentence is that a project company is a machine for manufacturing predictability out of a set of uncertain activities.
text: A company built to be predictable The special purpose vehicle exists to hold one project and nothing else. It typically has no employees, no premises and no operating capability of its own. Everything it needs is bought under a contract with a party better placed to provide it: construction from a contractor, operation from an operator, inputs from a supplier, and revenue from an offtaker or from users. The purpose of that arrangement is not efficiency in any ordinary sense. It is predictability. Each contract removes a source of variance from the vehicle’s cash flow by transferring it to somebody who can bear it, and what is left is a stream stable enough for lenders to advance seventy per cent of the cost against. B Gatti, ch. 1.4 and ch. 7.1; Delmon, ch. 3. 15

title: The contracts, and what each one removes
blockname: The special purpose vehicle and its contracts
notes: The last row is the one students skip and practitioners care about. A direct agreement is what makes step-in possible, and without it the lenders’ security is a claim over a company whose contracts have already gone.
text: The contracts, and what each one removes B Delmon, ch. 3.2; Gatti, ch. 7.2.6. 16 Contract Counterparty Variance it removes Concession or implementation agreement The contracting authority The right to build and operate, and the terms on which it can be taken away Construction contract, usually turnkey The contractor Cost overrun, delay, and performance on completion Operation and maintenance agreement The operator Operating cost and availability during the operating period Offtake or purchase agreement The offtaker Price and volume risk on what the project produces Input supply agreement The supplier Price, quantity and quality of what the project consumes Shareholders agreement The sponsors Governance, funding obligations and what happens when they disagree Financing agreements The lenders Drawdown, repayment, covenants and enforcement Direct agreements Lenders with each key counterparty The risk that a key contract terminates before lenders can intervene

title: The turnkey construction contract does the heaviest lifting
blockname: The special purpose vehicle and its contracts
notes: Interface risk is the concept to land. It is also why RE03 students will recognise the argument from the development process.
text: The turnkey construction contract does the heaviest lifting A turnkey, or engineering procurement and construction, contract places single-point responsibility on one contractor for design, procurement, construction and commissioning, at a fixed price and by a fixed date, with liquidated damages for delay and performance shortfall and a guarantee behind them. That is expensive. A contractor asked to carry that risk prices it, and the premium is real. Lenders insist on it anyway, because the alternative is that the vehicle carries interface risk between separate design and construction packages, and a vehicle with no employees cannot manage interfaces. This is the clearest example in the module of paying a party to bear a risk because it can manage it and you cannot. B Gatti, ch. 3.2.1; Delmon, ch. 20. 17

title: Availability, offtake and the shape of revenue
blockname: The special purpose vehicle and its contracts
notes: The final line is the sentence to keep. Everything in a credit structure is an answer to it.
text: Availability, offtake and the shape of revenue A take-or-pay offtake obliges the buyer to pay whether or not it takes the output, which removes volume risk entirely and is the strongest form. A capacity and energy structure splits payment into a fixed capacity charge, which covers debt service and fixed costs, and a variable charge for what is used. An availability payment pays for the asset being available to a standard, with deductions for unavailability and poor performance, and no volume exposure at all. A merchant structure has no contract and the project sells into a market, which is equity risk and is very rarely financed at project finance leverage. The lender’s question in every case is the same: what is the minimum cash the project receives in a bad year, and does it cover debt service. B Delmon, ch. 22; Gatti, ch. 3.2.4. 18

title: Step-in, and why lenders want the project rather than the assets
blockname: The special purpose vehicle and its contracts
notes: This explains the high recovery statistic from week 3 mechanically rather than by assertion, and students find the connection satisfying.
text: Step-in, and why lenders want the project rather than the assets If a project fails, foreclosing on a half-built tunnel is worthless. What lenders want is the ability to keep the project alive under new management, which requires two things: security over the shares in the vehicle, so they can replace its owners without disturbing its contracts, and direct agreements with each key counterparty, obliging that party to continue and to give lenders a period to cure a default before terminating. This is why recovery rates on project finance debt are high. The lenders are not selling an asset into a distressed market; they are taking over a going concern with contracted revenue and finding somebody else to run it. B Delmon, ch. 2.8.8 and ch. 24.6.2; Gatti, ch. 7.2.4.9. 19

title: Who sponsors a project, and what each wants
blockname: The special purpose vehicle and its contracts
notes: The last card is the point. A consortium of financial investors and a consortium including the industrial user of the output are very different credit propositions with identical documentation.
text: Who sponsors a project, and what each wants Industrial sponsor Has a core business the project serves: a utility, an energy company, a manufacturer securing supply. Wants the asset to work, and will support it beyond the contract if it must. Contractor sponsor Builds the project and takes equity to win the construction contract. Its return is substantially earned in construction, which is a conflict lenders watch closely. Public sponsor A state entity pursuing a welfare objective, often holding a minority stake to retain influence and information. Financial investor An infrastructure fund or institution with no operating role, seeking a return and an exit. Will not support the project beyond its contractual obligation. Operator sponsor Runs the asset and takes equity to secure the operating contract. Aligned during operation, and a weak counterparty in construction. Why the mix matters Lenders read the shareholder register as a statement about who will still be there when something goes wrong. B Gatti, ch. 1.3. 20

title: The advisers around the vehicle
blockname: The special purpose vehicle and its contracts
notes: This is the deliberate hand-off to week 5. Name the cast here and evaluate them next week.
text: The advisers around the vehicle A project financing requires legal advisers for the sponsors, for the lenders and often for the authority, an independent engineer reporting to lenders on technical matters, an insurance adviser, a model auditor, a market consultant to validate demand or resource assumptions, and financial advisers on both sides. The cost is substantial and it is not decoration. Each adviser exists to give one party independent assurance about a matter it cannot verify itself, which is a direct response to the information asymmetry that makes the transaction difficult. Week 5 asks what that assurance is actually worth, and whether the fee corresponds to it. B Gatti, ch. 4. 21

title: The security package, and what lenders actually take
blockname: The special purpose vehicle and its contracts
notes: Ask which item lenders would give up last. The answer is the share pledge together with the direct agreements, because between them they deliver control of a going concern.
text: The security package, and what lenders actually take A pledge over the shares in the project company, which allows lenders to replace the owners without disturbing the contracts. Security over the project’s receivables, so revenue is captured at source. Security over the project accounts, which is what makes the waterfall enforceable. Mortgages or equivalent over the project property, more useful as a blocking right than as a realisable asset. Assignment of the project agreements and of insurance proceeds. Direct agreements with each key counterparty, which convert all of the above into a workable ability to step in and continue. B Gatti, ch. 7.2.4; Delmon, ch. 2.3. 22

title: Conditions precedent, and why nothing is effective until everything is
blockname: The special purpose vehicle and its contracts
notes: Practitioners will recognise this immediately. Students find the all-or-nothing structure counter-intuitive until it is explained as a commitment problem.
text: Conditions precedent, and why nothing is effective until everything is Financial close occurs when a long list of conditions is satisfied simultaneously: contracts executed, consents obtained, land secured, insurance bound, security perfected, legal opinions delivered, equity commitments in place, and the base case model agreed and audited. The list is long because every party is unwilling to be committed while any other is not. That produces a characteristic pattern in which the transaction appears stalled for months and then completes in a single day, and it is why a slipping condition precedent, however minor, can hold an entire financing. B Gatti, ch. 7.2.3.4; Delmon, ch. 2.8.5. 23

title: Block B discussion
blockname: The special purpose vehicle and its contracts
notes: Question three works well in small groups and produces genuine disagreement about whether the offtake or the construction contract matters more.
text: Block B discussion Seminar questions A project company has no employees. What does that imply about who actually bears operational risk, and about what the sponsor is being paid for? A turnkey contract is more expensive than separate design and build packages. Who benefits from the premium, and would you pay it if you were funding the project with your own money? Rank the eight contracts by how much a lender would care if it were weak. Defend the top two. B 24

title: Risk identification and allocation
blockname: Risk identification and allocation
notes: The analytical centre of the week. Build the risk matrix with the students rather than presenting it.
text: Block C Risk identification and allocation What can go wrong, who should carry it, and what happens when the answer is nobody. Indicative length 40 minutes 25

title: Risks by project phase
blockname: Risk identification and allocation
notes: Gatti’s three-way split by phase is more useful than an alphabetical list because it maps onto the hazard shape from week 3. Risk is concentrated before completion and the structure exists to get past that point.
text: Risks by project phase C Gatti, ch. 3.1; Delmon, ch. 16. 26 Phase Principal risks Usual bearer Pre-completion Planning and consent, land, technology, construction cost and delay, performance on commissioning Contractor, with sponsor support and, for consent, the authority Post-completion Operating cost, availability, maintenance and lifecycle, input supply, demand and price Operator, offtaker, supplier, and the party best able to influence demand Throughout Interest rate, exchange rate, inflation, environmental and social, regulatory and political, force majeure, counterparty credit Hedged, shared, or retained by the authority where it is created by the state

title: The principle, and how often it is ignored
blockname: Risk identification and allocation
notes: Connect to week 2 block F. Transferring an unmanageable risk buys an option that will be exercised through renegotiation.
text: The principle, and how often it is ignored A risk should sit with the party best able to influence its likelihood or its consequences, and where nobody can influence it, with the party that can absorb it at least cost. That is the whole of risk allocation theory and it is easy to state. It is ignored constantly, in a predictable direction. Public authorities transfer risks the private party cannot manage, principally demand and policy risk, because transfer looks like prudence. The private party prices the risk, or fails to and renegotiates later. Either way the authority pays, and in the second case it pays at the worst moment. C Delmon, ch. 16.1; Ke, Y., Wang, S., Chan, A. P. C. and Lam, P. T. I. (2010), International Journal of Project Management 28(5), 482–492. 27

title: What practitioners actually think
blockname: Risk identification and allocation
notes: Give students the categories and ask them to allocate before showing the answers. The disagreements are where the learning is.
text: What practitioners actually think Delphi Method used by Ke and colleagues to establish preferred risk allocation in Chinese public private partnership projects. Rather than assert a risk matrix, the authors ran a two-round Delphi survey with experienced practitioners and recorded where consensus lay. The pattern is clear. The public sector is expected to take sole responsibility for expropriation and nationalisation, and the majority of responsibility for a further twelve risks connected to government and the actions of officials. Fourteen risks that neither side can control alone are preferred to be shared equally. The private sector is expected to carry the majority of ten project-level risks. The value for teaching is that students get an empirical risk matrix to argue with rather than a normative one to accept. C Ke and others (2010), International Journal of Project Management 28(5), 482–492. 28

title: The risks that are hardest to place
blockname: Risk identification and allocation
notes: The last item is genuinely current. Force majeure drafting changed materially after 2020 and again as physical climate risk has become quantifiable, which is a week 7 link.
text: The risks that are hardest to place Demand. Neither party controls it in most transport projects, so the question is who absorbs it more cheaply, and a diversified state usually can. Change in law. Created by the state, so in principle the state’s, but a general change affecting all businesses is not obviously the project’s to be compensated for. Land and consent. Usually the authority’s, because only the authority has compulsory powers, and a project that begins before land is secured has an unmanaged exposure. Inflation. Shared through indexation, and the detail of which index and what share of revenue matters more than the principle. Currency. Rarely allocable at a sensible price in the markets that need it most, which is the week 3 barrier appearing as a contract problem. Force majeure and its modern cousins, including pandemic and extreme weather, which are increasingly negotiated rather than boilerplate. C Delmon, ch. 16.4 to 16.11. 29

title: Risk allocation is priced, and the price is visible
blockname: Risk identification and allocation
notes: This is the sentence that connects block C to block D. Do not move on until it has landed.
text: Risk allocation is priced, and the price is visible Every transfer has a cost. A contractor asked to carry ground conditions risk prices it, and the price appears in the construction sum. An offtaker asked to take volume risk prices it, and the price appears in the tariff. A lender facing residual risk prices it in the margin and the cover ratio it requires. The practical implication is that the risk matrix and the financial model are the same document seen from two angles. A student who understands this can look at a tariff and infer the risk allocation behind it, which is a genuinely useful skill and one the group project will reward. C Corielli, Gatti and Steffanoni (2010). 30

title: Environmental and social risk is a credit risk
blockname: Risk identification and allocation
notes: This is the strongest environmental policy link in the week. Regulation by lending, and it binds where domestic regulation does not.
text: Environmental and social risk is a credit risk Lenders to infrastructure apply environmental and social standards, most commonly the Equator Principles and the IFC Performance Standards, which cover impact assessment, labour, resource efficiency, community health, land acquisition and involuntary resettlement, biodiversity, indigenous peoples and cultural heritage. The reason is not primarily ethical. A project that has not managed its social impact faces delay, litigation, protest and, in the limit, withdrawal of consent, all of which are credit events. Land acquisition and resettlement in particular have stopped more projects than technical failure has. For the environmental policy students this is the point at which the standards they study become a financing condition rather than an aspiration. C IFC Performance Standards and the Equator Principles; EP07 week 8, private governance of environmental problems. 31

title: Political risk, and its forms
blockname: Risk identification and allocation
notes: Creeping expropriation is the form that matters most in practice and the hardest to insure, because each individual act is defensible and only the pattern is confiscatory.
text: Political risk, and its forms C Delmon, ch. 16.8; Gatti, ch. 3.1.3.7; Hainz and Kleimeier (2012). 32 Form What happens Usual mitigation Expropriation The asset is taken, with or without compensation Political risk insurance; multilateral participation Creeping expropriation Tariffs frozen, permits withheld, taxes changed until the return disappears Contractual change in law protection; arbitration Transfer and convertibility Revenue cannot be converted or remitted Offshore accounts; insurance; local currency debt Breach of contract The authority does not perform and cannot be compelled Direct agreements; multilateral lenders; arbitration awards Political violence War, civil disturbance, terrorism Insurance, where available at a price Non-honouring of a guarantee A sovereign undertaking is simply not met Multilateral guarantee; preferred creditor effect

title: Insurance as a risk transfer instrument
blockname: Risk identification and allocation
notes: The last bullet is the analytical point. Insurance handles insurable risk, and what remains after it is where the equity return is actually earned.
text: Insurance as a risk transfer instrument Construction all risks and delay in start-up cover during the build, which is what protects debt service if completion slips for an insured reason. Operational property damage and business interruption cover once the asset is running. Third party liability, and environmental liability where available. Political risk insurance for the exposures on the previous slide, from public agencies and from a private market. Insurance is a transfer to a party that pools the risk, which is the efficient bearer principle in its purest form, and lenders specify the cover as a condition rather than leaving it to the sponsor. What insurance cannot cover is the interesting residual: demand, policy, and the expiry of a contract. C Gatti, ch. 4.3; Delmon, ch. 24.5.4. 33

title: Force majeure and change in law
blockname: Risk identification and allocation
notes: A pandemic tested every force majeure clause written before 2020 and most were found wanting. Physical climate risk is now testing them again, which is a week 7 connection.
text: Force majeure and change in law Force majeure covers events outside the control of either party that prevent performance. The drafting question is not whether to include it but what it does: suspend obligations, extend the concession, trigger compensation, or permit termination, and after how long. Change in law is treated separately because it is not outside the control of both parties. The state creates it, so a general change affecting all businesses is usually left with the project while a discriminatory change specific to the project or its sector is compensated. That distinction is easy to state and endlessly argued over, and it is where a great many disputes originate. C Delmon, ch. 16.8.4 and ch. 24.5.2. 34

title: Block C discussion
blockname: Risk identification and allocation
notes: Question three is the sharpest and the answer is yes, but only where the transferee genuinely manages the risk rather than merely holding it.
text: Block C discussion Seminar questions Allocate the risks for a greenfield toll road in a middle income country. Where would you deliberately depart from the Ke consensus, and why? An authority transfers demand risk to a concessionaire that cannot influence demand. Trace what happens over the following ten years under a pessimistic traffic outturn. If risk allocation is priced, is a heavily transferred structure ever cheaper for the state than a lightly transferred one? Under what conditions? C 35

title: Sources of funds and the capital stack
blockname: Sources of funds and the capital stack
notes: Gatti chapter 6 is the source. Work through the stack from the bottom up and keep referring back to the waterfall.
text: Block D Sources of funds and the capital stack Equity, mezzanine, senior debt and bonds, and how the stack is actually assembled. Indicative length 40 minutes 36

title: The capital stack
blockname: Sources of funds and the capital stack
notes: Shareholder loans are worth explaining. Much of what looks like equity is structured as subordinated debt for tax and distribution flexibility, which matters when students try to compute an equity return from published accounts.
text: The capital stack D Gatti, ch. 6.7 to 6.9; Delmon, ch. 2.8. 37 Layer Who provides it What it is paid Where it ranks Senior debt Banks, institutional lenders, bondholders Margin over a benchmark, plus fees First, after operating costs Subordinated or mezzanine debt Specialist funds, sometimes sponsors Higher margin, sometimes with equity features After senior, before equity Shareholder loans The sponsors Interest, often for tax reasons Behind all external debt Equity Sponsors and financial investors Residual cash flow and exit value Last Public support The state or a development institution Nothing, or a below-market return Varies by instrument, and often first-loss

title: Debt is sized against cash flow, not against assets
blockname: Sources of funds and the capital stack
notes: Flag explicitly that week 6 does the arithmetic. Students should leave knowing the principle and expecting the mechanics.
text: Debt is sized against cash flow, not against assets In corporate lending the question is what the borrower is worth. In project finance it is what the project can service. Debt is sized so that projected cash available for debt service exceeds scheduled debt service by a required margin in every period, under a downside case rather than the base case. That required margin is the cover ratio, and it is the subject of week 6. For now the important point is directional: a project with more contracted revenue supports more debt at the same cost, which is why sponsors spend so much effort on the offtake, and why an uncontracted merchant project is financed at leverage a fraction of a contracted one. D Gatti, ch. 5.2 and 5.3. 38

title: The senior facilities students will meet
blockname: Sources of funds and the capital stack
notes: The last line is the point. Project finance permits a precision of structuring that is impossible where funds are fungible across a business.
text: The senior facilities students will meet The base facility, which funds the construction cost and is repaid from operating cash flow. A working capital facility for the operating period. A standby facility, drawn only if cost overruns occur, which is how completion risk is funded without over-sizing the base facility. A value added tax facility, bridging the timing difference between paying tax on construction and reclaiming it. A debt service reserve facility, which can substitute for a funded reserve account and is cheaper. Each exists because a project has a lumpy and predictable funding profile, which lets facilities be tailored far more finely than corporate lending allows. D Gatti, ch. 6.9. 39

title: Bonds against loans
blockname: Sources of funds and the capital stack
notes: The construction-then-refinance pattern is the single most common financing plan in the sector and worth stating as such.
text: Bonds against loans A project can borrow from banks or issue bonds, and the choice turns on four things. Bonds give longer tenor and fixed rates, and access to institutional investors who cannot lend directly. Loans give flexibility: they can be drawn as construction progresses, amended when circumstances change, and waived by a small group of lenders who understand the asset. Bonds require a rating, which means an external party must be persuaded, and they require negative carry if funds are raised before they are needed. The practical resolution in many transactions is to build with bank debt and refinance into bonds once construction risk has passed, which matches the instrument to the risk profile at each stage. D Gatti, ch. 6.11; Abor and others (2025), ch. 12. 40

title: Islamic finance, briefly but properly
blockname: Sources of funds and the capital stack
notes: Given the cohort composition and the Gulf and Malaysian connections in the Department, this deserves more than a footnote. Keep it accurate and do not overclaim familiarity.
text: Islamic finance, briefly but properly Structures avoid interest and require that returns be linked to an identifiable asset or to a share in a real enterprise, which suits infrastructure unusually well. Debt-like contracts include murabaha, salam, istisna and ijara; participation contracts include mudarabah and musharakah. Sukuk are certificates representing an interest in an asset or venture rather than a debt claim, and are the principal capital markets instrument. For infrastructure the ijara and istisna structures map naturally onto construction and lease of a physical asset. The market matters practically as well as intellectually: several of the jurisdictions with the largest infrastructure programmes finance substantially in this form. D Gatti, ch. 6.12; Abor and others (2025), ch. 18. 41

title: Hedging, and what remains after it
blockname: Sources of funds and the capital stack
notes: The last sentence is the practical warning. Long-dated hedges are unavailable in exactly the markets that need them, which is the week 3 currency barrier restated.
text: Hedging, and what remains after it A project with floating rate debt and fixed contracted revenue has an interest rate exposure it cannot bear, so it swaps into fixed. A project with hard currency debt and local currency revenue has a currency exposure it usually cannot hedge for the tenor required. A project with an inflation-indexed tariff and nominal debt has a real exposure that varies with realised inflation. Hedging removes the exposures for which a market exists and leaves the ones for which it does not. Those residual exposures are where the real risk sits, and they should be identified explicitly rather than assumed away, because a hedge that terminates in year seven of a twenty-five year project has not solved the problem. D Gatti, ch. 3.1.3.3; Delmon, ch. 2.8.6. 42

title: When equity actually goes in
blockname: Sources of funds and the capital stack
notes: This is a good example of a structural feature that exists purely because of a conflict between two parties’ incentives, and students can derive it themselves if asked.
text: When equity actually goes in Sponsors prefer to contribute equity last, after debt has been drawn, because deferring the contribution raises the internal rate of return without changing anything real. Lenders prefer equity first, because money already spent is money that cannot be withdrawn when the project looks difficult. The usual compromise is a combination: some equity up front, the balance committed under a letter of credit or an equity contribution agreement, drawn pro rata or at the end. Where the balance is deferred, the lenders are in effect taking sponsor credit risk for the period, which is why the credit quality of the equity contribution agreement is scrutinised as carefully as the sponsor’s operating capability. D Gatti, ch. 6.7.1; Delmon, ch. 2.8.1. 43

title: The cost of capital for a project, and why it is not the sponsor’s
blockname: Sources of funds and the capital stack
notes: A tool import for the finance cohort and a genuinely common professional error. Worth ten minutes on the board.
text: The cost of capital for a project, and why it is not the sponsor’s A common error is to discount project cash flows at the sponsor’s weighted average cost of capital. The sponsor’s cost of capital reflects the risk of its existing business, and the project has a different risk. In a non-recourse structure the sponsor’s exposure is capped, and the project’s own capital structure is far more heavily geared than the sponsor’s. The correct approach is to build the project’s own cost of capital from the risk of its cash flows and its own gearing, and to recognise that gearing changes over the life of the project as debt amortises, so a single constant discount rate is an approximation whose limits should be stated. This is RE01 material applied to an entity with one asset and a declining debt profile. D RE01 sessions 3 and 4; Gatti, ch. 5.2. 44

title: Refinancing, and who gets the gain
blockname: Sources of funds and the capital stack
notes: The last bullet is the transferable idea and it applies well beyond refinancing.
text: Refinancing, and who gets the gain Once construction risk has passed, the project is a better credit and can usually borrow more cheaply and for longer than at financial close. Refinancing captures that improvement, and the gain can be substantial: lower margin, longer tenor, and often a release of cash to shareholders. In a public contract the question is who owns the gain. Early PPP contracts left it entirely with the private party, which produced windfalls that became politically damaging. Modern contracts share refinancing gains with the authority, typically on a defined split, and require consent for refinancings that increase the authority’s termination exposure. The lesson generalises. A contract that does not anticipate an improvement in circumstances allocates that improvement by default, and the default is rarely the one the public side would have chosen. D Delmon, ch. 9.5.5; Gatti, ch. 6.9.8. 45

title: Block D discussion
blockname: Sources of funds and the capital stack
text: Block D discussion Seminar questions A project can be financed with bank debt or with a bond. Which would you choose for a greenfield renewable project, and would your answer change once it is operating? Debt is sized against a downside case. Who chooses the downside case, and what stops it from being chosen conveniently? A project hedges interest rate risk for ten years on a twenty-five year concession. What has it actually achieved? D 46

title: Procurement routes and how the deal is won
blockname: Procurement routes and how the deal is won
notes: The theory here is Bajari, McMillan and Tadelis, and it is unusually clean. Give it the time.
text: Block E Procurement routes and how the deal is won Auctions, negotiations, and the competition that produces the contract. Indicative length 30 minutes 47

title: Routes to award
blockname: Procurement routes and how the deal is won
notes: Competitive dialogue is the interesting one. It exists precisely for the case Bajari and colleagues identify, where the specification cannot be complete at the outset.
text: Routes to award E Delmon, ch. 8.4 to 8.6; APMG PPP Certification Guide, chapter 5. 48 Route When it works What it costs Open competitive tender Standardised requirements, several credible bidders, contract can be fully specified Long, expensive for bidders, and inflexible once launched Restricted or prequalified tender Complex requirements where capability must be screened first Narrows the field, and prequalification criteria can be gamed Competitive dialogue The authority knows the outcome it wants but not the solution Very long, and requires an authority capable of running it Direct negotiation A single credible counterparty, or genuine urgency No price discovery, and the hardest to defend afterwards Unsolicited proposal The proponent has something nobody else has No competition at all unless one is manufactured afterwards

title: Auctions are not always better
blockname: Procurement routes and how the deal is won
notes: This is the week’s contrast slide and it will surprise students, who arrive believing competition is always preferable. The finding is not that auctions are bad; it is that they are a poor instrument for incomplete contracts.
text: Auctions are not always better 2009 Bajari, McMillan and Tadelis on when competitive bidding underperforms negotiation in procurement. Using a dataset of private sector building contracts in northern California, they find that auctions perform poorly where projects are complex, contractual design is incomplete, and few bidders are available. The mechanism is that an auction suppresses the communication between buyer and seller that a complex project needs. The buyer cannot draw on the contractor’s expertise while designing, so the project is designed worse and amended expensively afterwards. The largest and most novel infrastructure projects are exactly the ones where specification is least complete and bidders are fewest, which is where the case for open tender is weakest and where procurement rules insist on it most firmly. E Bajari, P., McMillan, R. and Tadelis, S. (2009), Journal of Law, Economics and Organization 25(2), 372–399. 49

title: What makes a tender fail
blockname: Procurement routes and how the deal is won
notes: The market sounding point is practical and worth emphasising. Asking the market what it will bid for, before writing the documents, is close to free and routinely omitted.
text: What makes a tender fail Too few bidders, which is common in large infrastructure because bid costs run to millions and only a handful of consortia can absorb them. Bid costs that are not recognised, so bidders price the risk of losing into the bids they win. Requirements that change during the process, which resets bidder pricing and rewards those who anticipated the change. Evaluation on price alone, which selects the bidder most willing to be optimistic, and produces the renegotiation from week 2. A public sector team without the capacity to run the process, which produces delay, and delay drives bidders away. Market sounding is the cheapest insurance against most of these and is skipped more often than it is done. E Delmon, ch. 8.1 to 8.9. 50

title: Financial close, and what actually happens in the last month
blockname: Procurement routes and how the deal is won
notes: This slide covers the part practitioners consider most important and courses generally omit. Trevor D’Olier-Lees or the IFC guest can speak to it.
text: Financial close, and what actually happens in the last month Between preferred bidder and financial close sits a period in which the transaction is frequently at its most fragile. Conditions precedent must be satisfied, lenders complete diligence and issue final credit approvals, insurance is bound, land title is confirmed, and every document is executed in a sequence in which nothing is effective until everything is. Between bid submission and close the market can move, and a rise in the cost of debt during that window is a risk somebody carries. Who carries it should be settled at bid stage and often is not, which is why so many transactions are repriced immediately before signature. E Delmon, ch. 8.10; Gatti, ch. 6.1.2. 51

title: The bidder’s economics, and why they shape the market
blockname: Procurement routes and how the deal is won
notes: Bid cost contributions, standardised documents and shorter processes are the practical levers. This is also a good answer to the two-bidder question in the discussion.
text: The bidder’s economics, and why they shape the market Bidding for a large infrastructure concession costs millions and takes a year or more, and the probability of winning against three competitors is one in four. A rational bidder therefore requires that the expected value of winning covers four bid costs, and prices accordingly. Two consequences follow. Bid costs are paid by the winning project and ultimately by users or taxpayers, so a process with many bidders is not free. And only consortia with the balance sheet to absorb repeated losses can participate, which is why the same names appear in every shortlist. An authority that wants more competition has to reduce the cost of bidding rather than exhort more firms to try. E Delmon, ch. 8.8. 52

title: Designing evaluation criteria
blockname: Procurement routes and how the deal is won
notes: The Hart connection is worth making explicitly: evaluation criteria are only as good as the specification, and the specification is only possible where quality is contractible.
text: Designing evaluation criteria Price alone selects the most optimistic bidder, which is the winner’s curse and then the renegotiation. Weighted quality and price requires the authority to define quality in advance, which is exactly the contractibility problem from Hart. A fixed tariff with competition on quality inverts the problem and works where the service is specifiable. Competition on a single financial variable, such as the required subsidy or the concession length, is transparent and easy to defend, and only works where everything else is genuinely fixed. Whatever the criteria, they must be published, applied as published, and capable of surviving challenge, because a procurement overturned late is more expensive than one designed slowly. E Delmon, ch. 8.6; Hart (2003). 53

title: Standardisation is the cheapest reform available
blockname: Procurement routes and how the deal is won
notes: The double-edge is the interesting part and it is an argument for periodic review of a standard rather than against having one.
text: Standardisation is the cheapest reform available Where an authority has a programme rather than a project, standardising the contract removes cost from every subsequent transaction. Bidders price a known document rather than reading a new one, legal fees fall, negotiation shortens, and the risk allocation becomes a policy decision made once rather than a negotiation conducted repeatedly by whoever is in the room. The United Kingdom’s standardised PFI contract is the best-known example and its lesson is double-edged. Standardisation delivered real savings, and it also propagated a risk allocation across hundreds of contracts, so that when the allocation turned out to be wrong it was wrong everywhere at once. E Delmon, ch. 13.5; APMG PPP Certification Guide, chapter 5. 54

title: Block E discussion
blockname: Procurement routes and how the deal is won
text: Block E discussion Seminar questions Bajari and colleagues find auctions underperform where contracts are incomplete. Public procurement rules generally require open tender for the largest contracts. How would you reconcile the two? A tender attracts two bidders. Should the authority proceed, and what would you do differently next time? Who should carry the risk that debt markets move between bid and financial close? E 55

title: Public support, guarantees and credit enhancement
blockname: Public support, guarantees and credit enhancement
notes: The block for the IFC guest. Keep the instrument-to-problem mapping visible.
text: Block F Public support, guarantees and credit enhancement What the state can add to make a transaction work, and what each addition costs it. Indicative length 30 minutes 56

title: Funded and contingent support
blockname: Public support, guarantees and credit enhancement
notes: The last row is deliberately last. Termination compensation is the single largest contingent exposure in most PPP portfolios and the one least often quantified.
text: Funded and contingent support F Delmon, ch. 10; Gatti, ch. 6.4 and 6.5. 57 Instrument Funded or contingent What it changes What it costs the state Capital grant Funded Reduces the cost to be recovered from tariffs Immediate and visible Availability payment Funded Removes demand risk entirely A long-dated commitment, recorded as such Concessional loan Funded Lowers the blended cost of capital The difference from market rate, rarely computed Minimum revenue guarantee Contingent Truncates the downside for equity and lenders A written option, usually unpriced Partial credit guarantee Contingent Raises the rating of the debt Contingent exposure to the full guaranteed amount Political risk insurance Contingent Covers expropriation, transfer and contract breach A premium, if bought commercially Termination compensation Contingent Makes the transaction bankable at all The largest exposure, and the least modelled

title: Credit enhancement, and what it is really doing
blockname: Public support, guarantees and credit enhancement
notes: This connects to the sovereign ceiling material from week 3. Enhancement is how a project pierces a ceiling, and it has a price that should be compared with the benefit.
text: Credit enhancement, and what it is really doing A partial guarantee from a highly rated institution raises the rating of a project’s debt, which widens the set of investors permitted to hold it. That is its purpose: not to make the project safer in any physical sense but to move it across a threshold in somebody’s mandate. Saying it that way is not cynical. Mandate thresholds are real constraints and moving across one genuinely changes the cost and availability of capital. But it does mean the value of the enhancement should be measured as the change in the cost of funds, against the expected cost of the guarantee to the guarantor, and that comparison is made much less often than it should be. F Gatti, ch. 8.2; Delmon, ch. 10.4. 58

title: Viability gap funding, and the discipline it requires
blockname: Public support, guarantees and credit enhancement
notes: Competing the subsidy is one of the genuinely good ideas in this field and it generalises: whenever the state must contribute, make the contribution the bid variable.
text: Viability gap funding, and the discipline it requires Many worthwhile projects cannot support their full cost from tariffs that users can pay. Viability gap funding closes that difference with a capital contribution, usually competed so that bidders compete on the smallest subsidy required. Competing the subsidy is what makes the instrument defensible: it reveals the minimum public contribution the market will accept rather than leaving it to negotiation. Where the gap is instead set administratively and then offered, the state has no way of knowing whether it paid too much, and the answer is usually yes. F Delmon, ch. 10.3.1; APMG PPP Certification Guide, chapter 4. 59

title: How a blended structure is actually assembled
blockname: Public support, guarantees and credit enhancement
notes: Ask which layer is doing the most work. It is usually the guarantee, because it changes who is permitted to invest rather than merely improving the return.
text: How a blended structure is actually assembled F Gatti, ch. 6.4 and 6.5; Broccolini and others (2021). 60 Layer Provider Function Grant for preparation Bilateral agency or facility Pays for the feasibility and transaction work nobody else will fund Viability gap capital grant The state Reduces the cost to be recovered from users Concessional senior or subordinated debt Development institution Lowers the blended cost of debt and lengthens tenor First-loss tranche Donor or climate fund Absorbs the initial losses that keep commercial investors out Guarantee Multilateral Raises the rating of the commercial tranche across a mandate threshold Commercial senior debt and equity Banks and funds The capital the structure exists to mobilise

title: Questions to put to the guest
blockname: Public support, guarantees and credit enhancement
notes: Send in advance. Question two is the one an economist wants answered and practitioners rarely volunteer.
text: Questions to put to the guest When you decide to participate in a transaction, what are you actually optimising, and how is that traded off against loss? How do you price a guarantee, and does the price reflect expected loss or the concessional intent? What proportion of the transactions you look at fail on the project and what proportion on the jurisdiction? Mobilisation is estimated at around seven dollars of commercial credit per dollar of multilateral lending. Does that match your experience, and what drives the variation? What would you change about how development institutions and commercial investors work together? F 61

title: Block F discussion
blockname: Public support, guarantees and credit enhancement
notes: Question one is the same exercise as week 3 block F and it is worth repeating, because students who could not do it then usually can by now.
text: Block F discussion Seminar questions A state gives a minimum revenue guarantee and records nothing. Value the guarantee as an option and say where it should appear in the public accounts. A partial credit guarantee moves a bond from sub-investment grade to investment grade. Estimate what that is worth in basis points and compare it with the expected cost to the guarantor. Should development institutions price at expected loss or below it? What follows for the market either way? F 62

title: Two cases
blockname: Two cases
notes: Gatti case studies 7 and 3. Set them as preparation and use the session for structured discussion rather than exposition.
text: Block G Two cases One advanced-economy renewable project, one emerging-market project bond. Indicative length 35 minutes 63

title: Why these two
blockname: Two cases
notes: Set both as preparation. Divide the room and have each half present the other’s risk allocation, which forces genuine reading.
text: Why these two The syllabus asks for project finance case studies in both advanced and developing economies, and Gatti supplies both in a form students can prepare from. Case study 7 is a solar power plant in Murcia, in a regulated European market, financed with senior bank debt against a power purchase agreement, with a hedging strategy, covenants and a base case built on an energy yield assessment. Case study 3 is the Odebrecht drilling project in Brazil, financed in the capital markets with an export credit agency refund guarantee, a cash waterfall, and step-in rights, in a jurisdiction and a sector where political and counterparty risk are material. Between them they cover almost everything in the week. G Gatti, case study 7 and case study 3. 64

title: The two cases side by side
blockname: Two cases
notes: Build this table with the students rather than showing it. It is the comparative review the syllabus asks for, in one exhibit.
text: The two cases side by side G Gatti, case studies 3 and 7. 65 Murcia solar Odebrecht drilling Jurisdiction Spain, an OECD regulated market Brazil, with offshore structuring Revenue Power purchase agreement Charter and service agreements with a single large counterparty Instrument Senior bank facility Project bond issued through a special purpose issuer Key support Market regulation and the offtake Export credit agency refund guarantees, equity support agreements Dominant risk Energy yield, price after the contract, regulatory change Counterparty concentration, political and country risk, construction What it teaches Debt sizing, covenants, hedging, sensitivity Capital markets execution, waterfall mechanics, credit enhancement

title: The questions to put to both cases
blockname: Two cases
notes: These five questions work on any project finance case and are worth giving students as a standing template.
text: The questions to put to both cases What is the minimum cash the project receives in a bad year, and what happens to the cover ratio then? Which party bears each of the six hardest risks from block C, and was that the efficient allocation? What happens when the revenue contract expires, and how much of the value rests on what happens afterwards? If this transaction had to be done again in a jurisdiction two notches lower, what would have to change? Where would you have refused to lend, and at what price would you have changed your mind? G 66

title: How to read a term sheet
blockname: Two cases
notes: This works well as a handout for the group project. Teams given a real term sheet and this table can produce a genuinely professional analysis.
text: How to read a term sheet G Gatti, ch. 7.2.3. 67 Section What to look for Why it matters Facilities and amounts Base, standby, working capital, and what each may fund Tells you what the lenders think might go wrong Tenor and repayment Final maturity against concession length, and the profile A tail between debt maturity and concession expiry is the lenders’ cushion Pricing Margin, step-ups, and fees Step-ups reveal where the lenders expect to be repaid or refinanced Financial covenants Cover ratio tests, lock-up levels, default levels The distance between lock-up and default is the equity’s room to manoeuvre Accounts and waterfall Reserve requirements and the order of payment Where the cash actually goes and when equity sees any Conditions precedent What must be true before a penny is drawn The practical critical path to financial close Events of default What triggers them, and what cure periods apply How quickly a difficulty becomes a crisis

title: The Italy water case, and where week 6 picks it up
blockname: Two cases
notes: Setting this in week 4 rather than week 6 makes the week 6 exercise much more productive. Say so explicitly.
text: The Italy water case, and where week 6 picks it up Gatti case study 2 is a full business plan for an integrated water system: timing, inflation, depreciation, interest, taxation, working capital, a debt service reserve, capital expenditure, sources of financing including a public grant, and an operating period covering the existing system, new supply and treatment works, and two hydroelectric plants. It closes on the economic and financial ratios. It is the only case in the set text that runs the numbers end to end, and it is the basis for the individual coursework in week 6. Students should read it now, so that when the modelling exercise arrives the transaction is already familiar and the work is analytical rather than descriptive. G Gatti, case study 2, and the appendix on the structure of the financial model. 68

title: Block G discussion
blockname: Two cases
text: Block G discussion Seminar questions Which of the two transactions was better structured, and by what criterion are you judging? The Odebrecht case relies on an export credit agency guarantee. Strip it out and re-price the transaction qualitatively. What survives? Both cases were financeable. Name a project you know of that would not be, and identify the single feature that makes it unbankable. G 69

title: Reserve material
blockname: Reserve material
notes: Not part of the two-hour session.
text: Block H Reserve material Slides held back from the main sequence. Indicative length As required 70

title: The financial model, and what week 6 will do with it
blockname: Reserve material
notes: A bridge slide to week 6. Useful to show at the end if time permits.
text: The financial model, and what week 6 will do with it A project financial model is the single document in which the risk allocation, the contracts and the capital structure all become numbers. It contains assumptions, capital expenditure, revenue, operating cost, tax, working capital, debt drawdown and repayment, reserves, and the resulting cash flows and ratios. It is built once and then negotiated over, and by financial close it is a contractual document rather than an analytical one. Week 6 builds and interrogates it. This week the point is only that everything discussed so far ends up inside it. Gatti’s appendix walks through the structure of a real model section by section and is the basis for the individual coursework. H Gatti, appendix. 71

blockname: Reserve material
notes: A note to the lecturer rather than a slide to show.
text: An alternative running order Where the cohort is drawn mainly from Real Estate Finance, compress blocks A and B, since capital structure and contract are familiar territory, and give the time to blocks C and E, where the material is genuinely new. Where the cohort is drawn mainly from Planning and Environmental Policy, invert: spend longer on A and B, treat block D as background, and use the EP02 instrument choice framing throughout block E so that procurement route selection is recognisable rather than technical. title: Where Week 4 leaves us
blockname: Reserve material
notes: Four sentences, one per block group.
text: Where Week 4 leaves us Project finance is the financing of a single-purpose entity against forecast cash flow, and every structural feature follows from that one choice. The contracts are not documentation. They measurably move loan spreads and gearing, which makes structuring a quantitative activity. A risk belongs with whoever can influence it, or absorb it most cheaply, and transferring it to anybody else buys an option that will be exercised. Competition improves procurement except where contracts are incomplete and bidders are few, which is precisely the case for the largest projects. 75
